questions.a: An operating system (OS) is system software that acts as an intermediary between computer hardware and the user, managing hardware and software resources and providing common services for application programs. It is a resource allocator (deciding which process gets which resource and when) and a control program (managing program execution to prevent errors and misuse). It also provides a convenient, efficient environment in which users can run programs.
questions.explanation: This captures the three classic roles of an OS: interface/abstraction over hardware, resource manager, and control program (the standard Silberschatz definition).
questions.oneShotPreview: OS = intermediary between hardware & users; resource allocator + control program + convenient execution environment.

questions.q: b) How is Computer systems divided? List and define.
questions.a: A computer system is commonly divided into four layers: (1) Hardware — the physical components (CPU, memory, I/O devices); (2) Operating System — the system software that manages hardware and provides services to programs; (3) System Programs — utilities and tools (shell, editors, compilers) that use OS services to support development and execution; and (4) Application Programs — end-user software that solves specific problems. This layered division shows where the OS sits between raw hardware and the user.
questions.explanation: The hardware -> OS -> system programs -> application programs hierarchy is the standard view of a computer system and clarifies the OS role.
questions.oneShotPreview: 4 layers: Hardware -> Operating System -> System programs -> Application programs.

questions.q: c) List and define the Operating system modes of operations
questions.a: Modern CPUs provide at least two modes: user mode and kernel (supervisor/monitor/system) mode. In user mode, applications run with restricted privileges and cannot execute privileged instructions or directly access hardware and protected memory. In kernel mode, the OS runs with full privileges and can execute any instruction and access any resource. A mode bit in the CPU indicates the current mode; switches occur through system calls, interrupts, and traps, which protects the OS and other users from a faulty or malicious program.
questions.explanation: Dual-mode operation with a mode bit is the fundamental hardware protection mechanism that lets the OS guard resources.
questions.oneShotPreview: User mode (restricted) vs Kernel mode (full privilege); mode bit switches via syscalls/interrupts/traps.

questions.q: d) What is a System Call?
questions.a: A system call is the programming interface through which a user process requests a service from the operating system kernel, such as creating a process, performing I/O, or accessing a file. It is the controlled mechanism that switches the CPU from user mode to kernel mode via a trap/interrupt at a defined entry point. To the programmer a system call looks like an ordinary function call (e.g., open(), read(), fork()), but it actually performs a protected transfer into the kernel.
questions.explanation: System calls are the gateway between user programs and kernel services and the primary cause of mode switches, central to both protection and service delivery.
questions.oneShotPreview: System call = user program's controlled request into kernel (trap -> mode switch) for OS services.

questions.q: e) What is Booting? List and define its types.
questions.a: Booting is the process of starting a computer and loading the operating system into main memory so that it can take control of the machine. The initial bootstrap program (firmware such as BIOS or UEFI) is stored in ROM and locates and loads the OS kernel. The two main types are cold booting — starting the machine from a powered-off state, including the Power-On Self-Test — and warm booting — restarting an already-powered system (e.g., a reboot) without a full hardware test. Modern systems may also use a multi-stage boot loader and secure boot.
questions.explanation: Booting bridges hardware power-on to a running OS; the cold/warm distinction is based on whether hardware is powered up from scratch.
questions.oneShotPreview: Booting = load OS via bootstrap (BIOS/UEFI); types: cold (power-on, full POST) and warm (restart).

questions.q: a) List and discuss the different functions of an operating system
questions.a: The main functions of an OS are: process management (creation, deletion, scheduling, synchronization, communication); memory management (allocation/deallocation, virtual memory); file management (files, directories, access control); device management (drivers, buffering, I/O scheduling); secondary-storage management (disk allocation, RAID); protection and security (access control, authentication); networking; and a user interface (CLI/GUI) plus system calls. It also performs accounting, error detection, and resource allocation. Together these functions make the system efficient, safe, and convenient to use.
questions.explanation: These are the standard OS functions; discussing each covers resource management, protection, and user convenience.
questions.oneShotPreview: OS functions: process, memory, file, device & storage management + protection, networking, UI, accounting/error handling.

questions.q: b) Explain different operations performed by the operating system.
questions.a: The OS performs operations such as process creation and termination, process scheduling and context switching, interprocess communication and synchronization, memory allocation and deallocation (paging/swapping), file operations (open, read, write, close), device I/O with buffering and caching, filesystem mounting, and protection checks. When an interrupt or system call occurs it saves the current context, dispatches the appropriate handler, and restores context afterward. It also detects errors, keeps accounting data, and maintains system state. These operations are triggered by user requests, hardware interrupts, or timer events.
questions.explanation: This describes the actual runtime operations the kernel executes in response to calls and interrupts, as distinct from its high-level roles.
questions.oneShotPreview: OS ops: create/schedule processes, context switch, allocate memory, file & I/O ops, protect, handle interrupts/errors.

questions.q: 3 Discuss the types of Operating System in detail. [L2][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: Major OS types include: batch systems (collect and run jobs without user interaction using job control language and spooling); multiprogramming systems (keep several jobs in memory to maximize CPU utilization); time-sharing/multitasking systems (many users share the CPU by rapid switching for interactive response); multiprocessing systems (multiple CPUs); distributed systems (networked computers cooperating as one); real-time systems (hard or soft timing guarantees, e.g., embedded control); embedded systems (specialized, resource-constrained, dedicated function); and personal/mobile, network, and cluster systems. Each type trades off responsiveness, utilization, determinism, and complexity.
questions.explanation: A detailed 10-mark answer should enumerate and explain each classic category along with its goal and defining characteristics.
questions.oneShotPreview: OS types: batch, multiprogrammed, time-sharing, multiprocessing, distributed, real-time, embedded, mobile/network.

questions.a: Computing environments include: traditional standalone/desktop systems; client-server systems (clients request services from servers); peer-to-peer systems (peers share resources directly); distributed systems (multiple machines cooperate over a network); centralized systems (one main host); real-time and embedded environments; mobile computing; cloud computing (virtualized, on-demand resources over the internet); grid and cluster computing; and virtualization, where multiple OS instances run on one physical machine. Each environment changes how resources, users, and processes interact and what the OS must manage.
questions.explanation: The question asks for the spectrum of environments in which modern operating systems operate, from a single machine to virtualized/cloud settings.
questions.oneShotPreview: Environments: standalone, client-server, P2P, distributed, centralized, real-time/embedded, mobile, cloud, virtualized.

questions.q: a) Define Free and Open-Source Operating Systems. How does Open-Source Operating System work? List the Advantages and Disadvantages of Open-Source Operating System.
questions.a: Free software is software users can run, copy, distribute, study, modify, and share freely — freedom, not necessarily zero price. Open-source software has publicly available source code under a license (e.g., GPL) permitting use, modification, and redistribution. An open-source OS such as Linux is built collaboratively: contributors submit code, maintainers review and merge it, and releases are published; users can inspect, patch, and customize the kernel. Advantages include low/no cost, security through peer review, high customizability, portability, community support, and freedom from vendor lock-in. Disadvantages include a steeper learning curve, less formal support/accountability, possible driver or hardware compatibility gaps, and fragmentation among distributions.
questions.explanation: This covers definitions, the community-based development model, and a balanced list of pros and cons, with Linux as the canonical example.
questions.oneShotPreview: Free = freedoms; open-source = source available. Community-driven dev. Pros: cheap, secure, customizable; cons: learning curve, support, drivers.

questions.q: b) Analyze the User and Operating-System Interfaces available
questions.a: OS interfaces split into user interfaces and the programming (system-call) interface. User interfaces include command-line interfaces (CLI/shell such as bash, where users type commands) and graphical user interfaces (GUI with windows, icons, menus, and pointing), plus modern touch and voice interfaces. The operating-system interface proper is the system-call interface/API (e.g., POSIX, Win32) through which programs request kernel services. A CLI is powerful, scriptable, and low-overhead but requires learning commands; a GUI is intuitive for beginners but consumes more resources and is harder to automate; the system-call interface is the essential programmatic boundary to the kernel.
questions.explanation: This analyzes the two user-facing interface styles, contrasts them, and identifies the program-facing system-call interface.
questions.oneShotPreview: Interfaces: CLI (powerful, scriptable) vs GUI (intuitive, resource-heavy); program interface = system calls/API.

questions.q: 6 List and explain the common services provided by an operating system with neat diagram. [L2][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: Common OS services are: program execution (load and run programs); I/O operations (handle input/output devices); file-system manipulation (create, delete, read, write, directories); communications (processes exchange data via messages or shared memory); error detection (detect and report hardware/software errors); resource allocation (allocate CPU time, memory, files, devices); accounting (track resource usage); and protection and security (access control and authentication). In a typical layered diagram, users and application programs sit at the top and call down into this service layer, which in turn uses the kernel and hardware below. These services are exposed to programs through system calls.
questions.explanation: These are the canonical OS services; describing the layered diagram shows where each service sits relative to users, programs, and hardware.
questions.oneShotPreview: Services: program execution, I/O, filesystem, communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting, protection/security.

questions.q: a) Explain why you need system calls in Operating System and how they work. [L2][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: System calls are needed because user programs run in user mode and cannot directly access privileged hardware or kernel data structures, so a controlled, protected gateway is required to request OS services and ensure consistent resource management and security. When a program invokes a call through a library wrapper (e.g., printf leading to write), a trap instruction switches the CPU to kernel mode and transfers control to a system-call handler selected by a call number in a system-call table. The kernel validates and executes the requested service, returns a result and status, then restores user mode and returns to the caller; parameters are passed via registers, a table, or the stack. This mechanism protects the OS, supports multiprogramming, and gives every program a uniform interface to hardware.
questions.explanation: This explains both the motivation (protection and abstraction) and the complete mechanism (trap, mode switch, dispatch, execution, return) of system calls.
questions.oneShotPreview: Need syscalls for protection + services; trap -> kernel mode -> handler via call number -> execute -> return to user mode.

questions.q: b) Evaluate the importance of system programs in the computing environments. [L5][CO1] [5M]
questions.a: System programs (system utilities) provide a convenient environment for program development and execution by building on OS services; examples include file management tools, status/information utilities, file editors, programming-language support (compilers, interpreters), program loading and execution facilities, communication tools, and command interpreters (shells). They bridge the raw system-call interface and the user, hiding low-level complexity and increasing productivity. Their importance lies in letting users manage files and processes, supporting software development, and being extensible with new utilities; they run as user-level processes distinct from the kernel itself.
questions.explanation: System programs are the user-facing utilities built on OS services; evaluating their role shows why they are vital for usability and development.
questions.oneShotPreview: System programs = utilities (shell, editors, compilers, file tools) built on OS services; make the system usable & productive.

questions.q: 8 Analyze the different types of System calls available in OS [L4][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: System calls are broadly categorized into: process control (create/terminate process, load and execute a program, wait for an event, get/set process attributes); file management (create, delete, open, close, read, write, reposition, get/set file attributes); device management (request/release device, read/write device, get/set device attributes, attach/detach); information maintenance (get/set time, get system or process/file/device information); communications (create/delete connections, send/receive messages, get/set connection attributes); and protection (get/set file permissions, allow/deny user access). Some systems also provide windowing and multimedia calls. Each category gives programs controlled access to a different class of resources.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark answer must enumerate and analyze the standard categories of system calls with representative examples for each.
questions.oneShotPreview: Syscall types: process control, file mgmt, device mgmt, information maintenance, communication, protection.

questions.q: 9 Imagine you're developing a lightweight open-source operating system. What key design goals would you prioritize, and how would you implement them? [L2][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: Key goals for a lightweight open-source OS are a small memory/CPU footprint, modularity, portability, security, power efficiency, and standards compliance. I would implement them by using a microkernel or modular design with loadable modules to keep the core small; coding in a safe, efficient language (C/Rust); providing virtual memory and demand paging only where needed; exposing a minimal POSIX-like API; using a clear layered architecture; shipping a small set of system programs and a package manager; adding a hardware abstraction layer for portability; and using a simple scheduler suited to light workloads. For the open-source aspect, I would use a permissive license, thorough documentation, automated testing, and security review to encourage community contributions.
questions.explanation: This maps each stated design goal to a concrete implementation strategy, which is exactly what the question asks.
questions.oneShotPreview: Goals: tiny footprint, modular, portable, secure. Implement: microkernel/modules, safe language, HAL, POSIX API, docs + community.

questions.q: a) Design a boot sequence for an operating system and outline the steps involved in system start up. [L6][CO1] [5M]
questions.a: A typical boot sequence is: (1) Power-on — the CPU begins executing firmware (BIOS/UEFI) from ROM at the reset vector. (2) POST — the Power-On Self-Test checks memory, CPU, and devices. (3) Firmware discovers boot devices and loads a boot loader (e.g., GRUB) from the boot sector or EFI partition. (4) The boot loader loads the kernel image into RAM (with an optional initrd/initramfs) and transfers control to it. (5) The kernel initializes memory management, interrupts, scheduling, and drivers, then mounts the root filesystem. (6) The kernel starts the first user process (init/systemd), which runs startup scripts, starts services, and presents a login prompt or desktop. Control thus passes from firmware to boot loader to kernel to user space.
questions.explanation: This outlines the standard firmware -> boot loader -> kernel -> init chain and the key initialization at each stage.
questions.oneShotPreview: Boot: power-on -> POST -> firmware loads bootloader -> load kernel -> kernel init -> init/systemd -> login.

questions.q: b) How would you use log files, core dumps, and trace listings to debug a system that is intermittently failing? [L2][CO1] [5M]
questions.a: For intermittent failures I would first enable detailed, timestamped logging (syslog/journal) and centralize logs to correlate the failure time with errors and device events, adjusting log levels as needed. When a crash occurs I would analyze the core dump with a debugger such as gdb to inspect memory, registers, and the call stack at the moment of failure, pinpointing the exact instruction and state. I would also capture trace listings — system-call traces (strace), kernel traces (ftrace/perf), or event traces — to reconstruct the sequence of calls and interrupts leading to the fault. Correlating timestamps across the logs, the core-dump stack, and the event trace reveals the triggering sequence; for rare events I would add targeted instrumentation to narrow the time window and confirm the root cause.
questions.explanation: This explains the distinct contribution of each diagnostic artifact and how correlating them isolates an intermittent bug.
questions.oneShotPreview: Correlate timestamps in logs + analyze core dump stack + trace syscalls/events -> find root cause of intermittent fault.

questions.q: 11 Illustrate any two operating system structures. [L3][CO1] [10M]
questions.a: Two common OS structures are: (1) Monolithic structure — the OS is one large program in which all services (process, memory, file, device management) run in kernel mode and call one another directly; it is efficient but harder to maintain and a single bug can crash the system (e.g., traditional UNIX, Linux). (2) Microkernel structure — only a minimal core (IPC, scheduling, basic memory) runs in kernel mode while most services such as the file system and drivers run as user-level servers communicating by message passing; it is modular, secure, and extensible but incurs message-passing overhead (e.g., Mach, MINIX, QNX). A diagram would contrast a single large kernel block with a small kernel surrounded by user-level servers. Other structures include layered, modular, and client-server designs.
questions.explanation: A 10-mark answer should illustrate two structures with their organization, advantages/disadvantages, and examples.
questions.oneShotPreview: Monolithic (all services in kernel, fast but fragile) vs Microkernel (minimal kernel + user servers, modular but slower IPC).
